LESSON 94 OF 106·Defensive Operations: Detect, Respond, Recover

Forensics Basics and Evidence Handling

Acquiring, preserving and working with evidence: why a verifiable copy matters, what order of volatility is for, and how a defensible record is built from the moment you touch a system.

Applied Foundation17 min
Why this matters

Forensics is what you do with the data you preserved. The order of operations matters enormously, because the first action taken often destroys the evidence you would have needed.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Live memory holds evidence that is gone the moment the machine powers off, so that decision comes first and is irreversible.
  • Imaging a running system is not perfect, which is why containment decisions have to be made consciously.
  • A write-blocked copy preserves the original; analysing the original directly is how evidence gets contaminated.
  • Hashing and timestamping establish an integrity record that survives a challenge later.
  • Chain of custody exists so the evidence is admissible, which is a legal requirement rather than a technical one.

The background

  • Early forensics was disk-level and destructive, which meant investigating meant destroying the evidence.
  • Write blockers and disk imaging made non-destructive analysis possible.
  • Memory forensics became practical and changed what could be recovered after a compromise.
  • Cloud and containerised systems changed the model again, because there is often no disk to image.

Real-world examples

  • Rebuilding a machine before imaging it destroys the memory and the temporary files that explained the intrusion.
  • Running antivirus on an infected host before imaging changes the very files being investigated.
  • Evidence held without a custody record can be excluded, however conclusive it was.

What to look for

  • Check whether your response plan starts with preservation, or with containment that destroys evidence.
  • Check whether you can acquire a full memory capture on the platforms you run.
  • Check whether the imaging and custody process is documented and repeatable.
  • Check whether you have somewhere to store evidence securely for as long as it may be needed.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

NIST SP 800-86 — Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

Reading how a national standards body frames the four forensic phases and the argument for integrating forensic practice into response rather than adding it afterwards

Open NIST resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Decide the preservation order in advance and write it into the playbook.
  • Capture memory before power-off on systems where that evidence matters, and accept the trade-off consciously.
  • Image with a tool that hashes as it writes, and keep the original read-only.
  • Record every transfer of evidence, with who handled it and when.
  • Practise acquisition on a lab machine, since the first real attempt should not be the first attempt.
